speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That standing order 63 be amended by striking out the -words "and international" in subsection (j) and adding after subsection (k): (1) On external affairs, to consist of 20 members, 8 of whom shall constitute a quorum.
He said: Hon. members will recall that it was suggested by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) a few days ago that the committee on industrial and international relations should be divided into two separate committees, one having to do with labour and industrial relations and the other with commonwealth and foreign relations-I think those are the words my hon. friend used. I mentioned that at a previous session of parliament the same suggestion had been made. It was, I think, by my hon. friend the leader of the C.C.F. group (Mr. Coldwell). At the time I intimated that that course might be advisable.
As I said the other day, I think it is desirable to have two separate committees, one on industrial relations and the other on external relations. I chose the words "industrial relations" and "external affairs" as being sufficiently comprehensive to include all that has

been suggested. The leader of the opposition suggested, if I remember rightly, a committee on "labour and industrial relations". Of course, labour is one party to industry, and by using the expression "industrial relations", other parties, which would include management, capital and the community, would be included. I should think the more comprehensive designation would be the preferable.
In regard to international relations my hon. friend suggested "commonwealth and foreign relations". Here again I feel that the term "international relations" or "external affairs" would be broader and would include everything which is suggested by "commonwealth and foreign relations". The term "external affairs" has been used by different governments of the commonwealth in dealing with matters pertaining not only to relations between the different nations of the commonwealth, but also with regard to matters that relate to foreign countries. It is important that the distinction should be kept between foreign affairs and those affairs that might be regarded as interimperial or commonwealth. But all are included in the term "external affairs". The term was used when the Department of External Affairs was created to cover both relations within the commonwealth and relations .ith foreign countries. I therefore feel it would be preferable to use the term "external affairs rather than commonwealth and foreign relations".
The conference which was held in London in 1926 drew up a statement of the relations as they now exist within the commonwealth, and^ defined the position which had been attained by the dominions as well as by the United Kingdom. In what is known as the Balfour declaration the term used is "domestic and external affairs," there being no subordination one way or the other between the dominions in regard to the control of their own affairs, whether domestic or external, and the United Kingdom and its control of its affairs, domestic or external.
In these circumstances I would suggest that to use the term "industrial relations" in the one case and "external affairs" in the other for the names of the two committees would be the more appropriate; and may I say that the government is only too happy to have these two committees established in place of the one which at present exists.

I am veiy glad to see this motion moved, and I think the Prime Minister's suggestion as to the naming of the committees is a good one. It seems to me accurately to portray what those committees should be concerned with.

Canadian Navy	______
But there is one phase of the motion which I want to draw to his attention-that it provides for only twenty members, eight of whom shall constitute a quorum. I think that this is a very important committee; more members of the house are interested in external affairs than in some of the other committees where the membership runs up to well over fifty. Indeed there is only one standing committee with a smaller number of members, and that is on debates, where we have twelve members.
The proposal for the industrial committee is, as I take it, that it remain at thirty-five members; and it seems to me that this very important committee on external affairs should have a membership at least equal to that of the industrial committee, because many members of the house will want to be on that committee.
Then, too, there are in the house at the present time several parties, all of whom will want some membership on that committee, and twenty, it seems to me, does not give the necessary representation.
I do not want to move that "20" be struck out and "35" substituted therefor. I believe that one has only to draw the matter to the attention of the Prime Minister and a satisfactory solution will be arrived at.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
May I say to
my hon. friend that after the notice was placed on the order paper the Clerk drew to my attention the fact that the numbers he had inserted were "20" and "8", and I really intended to mention that if the house wished to have a larger number, a larger number could be immediately substituted. With the consent of the house I would have "35" substituted for "20" and "10" for "8" in the resolution, which would make the membership of the external affairs committee the same as that of the committee on industrial relations. Motion as amended agreed to.

I wish to ask the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services a question in regard to a statement which appeared in the Vancouver Daily Province to the effect that recruiting for the navy was to be opened for 4,000 out of a post-war total of 12,000. It pointed out also that those who were applying were largely civilians, but that increasing numbers of those now being demobilized were anxious to get into the permanent naval service. Would 
the minister be good enough to make a statement with regard to this, as tcv whether it applies all over Canada and whether these recruits will enter direct into the Royal Canadian Navy or, as hitherto in recent years, into the volunteer reserve?

speakeroldname: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CONDITIONS OF POST-WAR RECRUITMENT
speechtext:
I did
not see the press item to which my hon. friend refers, but the position, as I think the house is aware, is this. A week or ten days ago-it may be two weeks-recruiting in all three services was authorized in what was referred to as an interim force, the term of enlistment to be for a period to expire on September 30, 1947. No definite number for these recruitments has been fixed, and so far no definite decision has been taken as to the size of the permanent force in any of the three services. The enlistments for these interim forces are being taken from those who are now serving. One of the main purposes in arranging for such enlistments now was to give men who might be interested in serving in the permanent forces after the war the assurance that over the next two years they would have a definite engagement and they would be able to decide, after the conditions and the size of the permanent forces were known, whether or not they would wish to serve in them. The statement which was issued at the time this type of enlistment was authorized indicated that men who enlisted for this special term would be given special consideration for enlistment in the permanent forces.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: SPECIAL BONUS FOR SERVICE IN DANGEROUS WATERS-S.S. "PRINCE EDWARD"
speechtext:
On Friday of last week the junior member for Queens (Mr. McLure) asked if the seamen on the steamship Prince Edward are entitled to the special bonus. Since then, and before, the senior member for Queens (Mr. Douglas) has also made representations on behalf of the same seamen. I have had inquiries made and am now able to reply to my hon. friends as follows.
The merchant seamen special bonus order, P.C. 3227 of the 3rd May, 1945, provides for the payment of a bonus of ten per cent of earnings of seamen serving on Canadian ships, who have performed at least six months' service in dangerous waters between September 10, 1939, and April 1, 1944.
The definition of "dangerous waters" means waters in respect of which war risk bonus is paid.
The seamen serving on the S.S. Prince Edward have been receiving war risk bonus by a ruling from the national war labour board which came into effect on February 26, 1943. The said seamen would therefore be entitled to the merchant seamen special bonus of ten per cent of their earnings from February 26, 1943 until April 1, 1944, upon making an application in the approved form to the director of merchant seamen, Department of Transport, Ottawa.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a feeling of trepidation that I rise to address the house for the first time, but having seen how well the other tyro members have done I am glad to jump in and join in the debate. In this my first address to the house I should like to emphasize the fact that I am an independent. I believe that there has been some discussion on that point. I believe that my ballot paper overseas was marked "Independent Liberal", but I should like to clear up that point and say that I am following along in the tradition of Comox-Alberni as a straight independent, and in my vote in the house I shall try to reflect the opinions and the wishes of the people of Comox-Alberni who sent me here.
The constituency of Comox-Alberni consists of the northern and western three-quarters of Vancouver island. It is the constituency of which Mr. Rudyard Kipling once said, in a masterpiece of understatement, that it was the fairest jewel in the British crown.
At this time I should like to pay a tribute to the gentleman whom I have the honour to succeed. I am quite certain that all the old-timers in this house will recall with great affection and high regard Mr. A. W. Neill, the former member for the constituency. I have been particularly pleased since I came to Ottawa to find in all groups and sections of
*JAS	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Gibson (Comox)
this house, and also among the civil service, that he was very affectionately regarded. As a matter of fact that is just the way we have always felt about Mr. Neill in Comox-Alberni, and I am particularly proud to be here to succeed him. I should like to tell the house at the same time that the only reason I am here succeeding him is that he did not choose to run again.
I should like to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, on your election to the high office of first commoner. I should also like to congratulate the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) and the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Langlois) on the able way in which they opened the debate. On behalf of the Liberals in the constituency of Comox-Alberni, I express my thanks to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and to the members of his cabinet for the able way in which they administered the affairs' of Canada during the past five years. 1 wish also to convey to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), who has taken over the reins of office, the very high regard in which he is held by the Conservatives of Comox-Alberni. To the hon. members of the Conservative party who were in opposition during the last five years I extend the thanks of my constituency for the able job they did at that time.
Now, coming to the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) I should like to say that a number of people in my constituency are adherents of his, and now that I have met the hon. gentleman I must say that I can well realize why he is held in affection by that large number of people-there were more than I expected on election day. He is very highly regarded there.
I come now to the Social Credit party. They have a new leader in the house, and I congratulate him on his election. I should also like to mention the former leader who was in the last parliament. I thank him on behalf of my constituency for the contribution that he made. I am sorry that the philosophy of social credit has not penetrated to the dark fastness of Comox-Alberni. I sincerely trust that my position here, adjacent to the hon. members, will allow me to acquire some of their philosophy.
I was particularly interested in the speech of the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Ashby). He made a suggestion that was very interesting to me. He said it was possible that we might pay an old age pension of $100 a month at age forty. In one more year I shall qualify for that. I was particularly interested as an independent, because the past tradition of independence in this house does

not lead me to believe that- I shall be put out into the lush pastures when I have lost my usefulness; therefore I really believe that he has something there that will interest me greatly.
I was disappointed when I read the speech from the throne, because of its obvious omission. I feel that I would not be maintaining the standards of Comox-Alberni if I did not point out that we were not told anything about our Japanese problem and the solution of it. Hon. members, of course, are accustomed to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni bringing up this vital point. Now that the government's dispersal policy has brought the problem into almost every constituency in Canada, I am hopeful that the British Columbia members-there are eleven of us to whom this is a most vital problem; the other five, of course, are "agin us"-will receive the support of other hon. members in the house.
I should like to make it very clear-and I am not going to take up a lot of time on the Japanese question now, because we shall have time to discuss the problem later-that our opposition 'o the Japanese in British Columbia is not based on the matter of race. If hon. members knew them as well as we do they would find that our opposition is based upon the fact-and I have lived among them for thirty years-that they are not loyal and never have been, and I do not expect they ever will be, to Canada. The Prime Minister felt that it was a wise course to appoint a quasi-judicial committee to look into the matter, but I believe the proper time to judge the loyalty of the Japanese citizens in this country was after Pearl Harbor-about a week after that-and at the time of Singapore, and at the time we lost the Prince of Wales and Repulse. . We could have decided then, and I believe we woidd have had many more of them who would have applied to return to Japan than will do so now after they have had Mr. Howe's atomic bomb.
I would be remiss in my duty to my constituents of Comox-Alberni and to the members of the government if I did not present a true picture of how we feel in our constituency -and I may say I have the temerity to speak for the other ten constituencies I mentioned- if I did not say that I believe the people of Comox-Alberni are definitely determined that the Japanese shall never return to British Columbia again.
I was glad to note yesterday that the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) injected into this debate the subject of the monopoly of the American Can company in British Columbia. As a canner in British Columbia I should like to bring before this

The Address-Mr. Gibson (Comox)
house some of the facts in that regard. I charge definitely that the American Can company could have prevented the loss of fish and vegetables at the time of the strike had they so desired. Make no mistake about it; they were definitely aware that this strike was coming. They could have provided every cannery in British Columbia with all the cans they required to put up all the food we had there at the time. Instead of taking that course they supplied the large canners in British Columbia. It is significant that at the time not one large cannery in the province ran out of cans. Because of the fact that the small canner3 did not find it possible to put up the necessarily large amounts of money required, they were unable to get a large stock of cans ahead to carry them through that strike. Speaking for our own cannery, we are 5,000 cases of salmon short in our pack this year because we did not have enough cans in storage prior to the strike. Definitely that was because the American Can company put their cash dividends and money matters ahead of the necessity of providing food for the people overseas; that is why we are now short a large part of our normal pack of salmon and vegetables in British Columbia. When I mention the figure of 5.000 cases I am referring to one cannery only. Numerous other small canneries were involved to the same extent. Five thousand cases represents 200.000 cans, which means salmon for 200,000 British families for one week. When you multiply that by possibly ten canneries of the size of ours, you can see that it will make a tremendous difference in the food supplies available to people overseas. I am particularly anxious that the small farmers and fishermen of British Columbia should never again find themselves in the position that this large United States monopoly will have a stranglehold on them, as has been the case in the past.
I am glad to see that our new Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bridges) has come into the house, and I particularly want to congratulate him on his appointment to this high office. I hope very soon he may be able to take time off to come out and visit us on the Pacific coast, where I can assure him he will receive a royal welcome. His predecessor as minister, the present Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) has left an enduring monument to his administration in the Hell's Gate fisheries project. I understand about a million dollars was spent there, but I can assure the house that this amount will be returned in new wealth every year as a result of the work done at that point. As yet I have not run into this mysterious treasury board which was mentioned
yesterday by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), but I sincerely trust that in future it will look with more favour upon the estimates of the Minister of Fisheries. Every time during the war years we asked the fisheries department to make any expenditures we were given the same answer, that there were more important things to do in connection with the war; and with that attitude I was largely in agreement. Now, however, the time has come when the fisheries department can make a valuable contribution to the economy not only of British Columbia but of Canada as a whole, and I should like to think that the regime of the new minister will come to be known as the golden age for the fisheries of my province.
Soon the budget speech will be brought down. I share with most Canadians a high regard for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) for the splendid job he has done. I should like to point out, however, that our present system is really one of incentive, and, that being so, as long as the excess profits tax remains in operation the incentive is taken away. I may be telling tales out of school, because I know the Department of National Revenue is highly efficient, but so often I have heard of someone who was said to be "taking a trip on Ilsley" or "buying a bottle of Scotch on Ilsley" and so on. Perhaps the Excess Profits Tax Act actually has worked against the best interests of Canada. I should also hope that in the new budget some reduction will be made in the taxes now imposed upon the small wage-earners; surely we can manage that. We should go ahead and finance this year for our ordinary expenditures, but I suggest that extraordinary expenditures in connection with demobilization, reconstruction and so on should be budgeted over a period of five years. You will note that I am expecting the government to remain in office for five years. If a proper job is done during this reconstruction period I should think it even possible that the government might last for ten years.
If I might make another suggestion to the Minister of Finance, I would point out that this year the income of the pilchard fishermen on the west coast of Vancouver island has been almost nil. It seems to me only fair that those engaged in industries where there may be such wide fluctuations should have the privilege of spreading their income over a three-year period and paying their taxes on that basis, just as we have done for those in the fishing industry and in agriculture.
There has been a good deal of discussion here in regard to housing, and in that connection mention has been made of the lumber
250	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Gibson (Comox)
shortage. I was glad to notice that finally, in response to requests from several hon. members on this side of the house, statements were made from the ministerial benches giving us some idea of what may be the policy of the government with regard to housing, which of course ties in with reconstruction. Two days ago I had a telephone call from a British Columbia lumberman advising me that he was short 150 employees. I should like to point out that his plant is only three hours' drive from Vancouver, where at the same time we had thousands of men demonstrating, asking for severance pay and a continuation of uneconomic industries so that they might not have to move out of town. This lumberman's plant is in a large town, which is just as modern as this city of Ottawa, so that there is no reason in the world why men should not move out to those jobs. When I refer to loggers and saw mill workers in British Columbia I should like hon. members to note that the average wage is around 80 cents an hour in our saw-mills and at least SI an hour in the logging camps, so that taking these jobs would not involve any great economic hardship.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about the homes for them to live in?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
They are close to the source of supply of lumber, in Port Alberni, and we can build them homes. I think the real solution of this problem must be for the people in the large cities, who have been drawn there to do war work, to get back to where our real primary wealth lies; that is, away from the great centres of population. Those are the places from which these people have come, and those are the places to which they will have to return.
When I speak of the lumber camps in British Columbia I should not like the house to get the impression which was conveyed the other day by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Archibald), who told the house that the loggers on the Queen Charlotte islands were living under the most primitive conditions. I have lived in logging camps for the last thirty years-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: So have I.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I think you spent most of your time in the post office.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I worked in the camps.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do not think you worked in the camps very much. I would have my hon. friend know that the accommodation and food in the logging camps of British Columbia are infinitely better than in the city of Ottawa. Any time hon. mem-

bers have an opportunity to come to British Columbia I shall be glad to give them a real logging camp meal. Only once since coming to Ottawa have I had anything to compare with it-and I must mention that occasion now because I see my host sitting here in the house. I can assure him, however, that I say this with great sincerity.
I should like to congratulate the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) upon his most able address delivered last night. But, if he does not mind my giving him a slight suggestion, I would say that he has a difficult job on his hands, in the vast department he administers, if he is going to try to run interference for every one of the, let us say, brass hats-I believe I have heard them called that-working under him in his department. I refer to brass hats both in and out of uniform.
The minister is a busy man, and I know, too, that he is very much overworked. Perhaps some time he would be able to come to Comox, and if he does I should like to take him fishing. I know that if he did that it would do him a tremendous amount of good, and provide him with the rest he so badly needs. While we are trolling along I will see that he gets some salmon, and I shall also take him and show him some charred hulks of valuable landing barges we have out there. I do not take the minister to task for this, because I know he has been extremely busy, but I would convey to him the thought that if occasionally some hon. members in the house question the disposal of war assets he ought not to run interference too readily. I believe him to be a man who is extremely loyal to the officials associated with him, and for that I honour him greatly. I suggest to him, however, that the real intention of hon. members sitting over here is that of being helpful, and that they have no desire only to be critical.
Many people have been bothering the Minister of Finance about meat rationing. Just how meat and money go together has always been somewhat of a mystery to me. I say to the minister, however, that the present meat ration when applied to logging camps in British Columbia is entirely inadequate. We hear talk about a man living on a pound and a third of meat per week, but those of us who buy meat to keep our commissaries supplied in the logging camps have found that it takes a pound of meat per man per day to supply their requirements. I do not think we should cut down the ration of those who are doing very heavy work. As a matter of fact, in a masterpiece of overstatement, one mar said that it was a day's work to walk around one of our trees. I suggest that some special

The Address-Mr. McKay
consideration should be given to the men in the logging camps who eat in the camp cook houses, and also to the people who, while occupied in that industry, live in their homes, and go from those homes to their work. They require substantial lunches, and need three heavy meals a day.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first congratulate the mover (Mr. Benidickson) and the seconder (Mr. Langlois) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Veterans generally will appreciate the recognition accorded the armed services by the selection of these two very fine young men to lead off the debate. I trust that veterans in the house on every side will cooperate in seeing that our returning service personnel are not only properly housed, but receive decent jobs; and also that those who are disabled as a result of war service receive not only compensation but satisfactory treatment for any injury so received.
I represent the constituency of Weyburn, and in being so selected I feel that I have been highly honoured. It is no easy task to follow in the footsteps of the former member for Weyburn, who is now premier of Saskatchewan, the Hon. T. C. Douglas. It is Weyburn, too, that was the home of the South Saskatchewan regiment, which so ably distinguished itself at the battle of Dieppe.
Most tseople are aware of the fact that Weyburn is a typical agricultural community. Because it is such, it is my purpose at this time to deal with certain facts pertaining to
agriculture, and to outline as briefly as I can some of the policies of the C.C.F. in regard to that major industry.
In spite of our vast war-time development, agriculture is still Canada's No. 1 industry. According to the 1941 census, twenty-five per cent of our workers are still following agricultural pursuits, while twenty-three per cent of the workers are engaged in other industries. Moreover, many of the workers in those other industries are employed in factories which, in order to operate successfully, must depend upon raw materials from the farms.
In a recent bulletin the Canadian association on adult education stated that 126,000 young people left the prairie provinces in recent years to seek outside those provinces employment in industries which are more remunerative than the industry they have been accustomed to serve, namely agriculture.
It is a tragic story that many of these people come from rural homes. The 1931 census, which dates back another ten years, reveals for the first time in our history that there were more people living in urban centres in Canada than there were in rural areas, and during the last decade the trend to the city has been definitely accelerated. Obviously that is a most serious situation. The basic reason, notwithstanding war conditions, is that farming is unattractive to a large part of our population. It holds out few inducements to our young people; and while it has been more profitable within the last few years, owing to a false condition of war prosperity, most farmers realize that it is far from a permanent period of prosperity.
Most young people and their farm parents are all too familiar with the vicissitudes of farm life. They recall all too vividly those distressing days when they received the pittance known as relief. I am sure all hon. members are aware that during the depression agriculture suffered a tremendous loss of income. I wonder just how many know that that loss of income amounted to two-thirds of what it was in normal times. Between 1928 and 1933 it went even lower than that. Many do not realize that since the last war the farmer has never received a fair share of the national income. His share is still too low, even* now, in relation to other sections of our population. In normal times one-third of our people live on the farms, but never since the last war have the farmers received one-third of the national income. During the decade 1930 to 1940, not so long ago, that income fell to one-tenth of the national income. It is obvious, then, that so long as farm folk receive this inadequate share of the national income there will be difficult days for agriculture.
The Address-Mr. McKay

The advisory committee on reconstruction has expressed itself thus regarding agricultural policy:
Agriculture cannot be made attractive to those seeking a means of living unless it can be restored to its historic position of selfdependence and self-respect. The price received by the farmer for his products must be such as will maintain a standard of living comparable to that enjoyed by urban communities and adequate to supply farmers and their families with the ordinary conveniences and comforts of life.
Prosperity for agriculture definitely depends on world markets. The United nations conference on food and agriculture, which met in the United States in 1943, stated:
The world's agriculture must be organized and expanded to provide enough of the right kind of food for everyone.
Statements emanating from the San Francisco conference were to the effect that two-thirds of the world's present population is still underfed. Contrary to the belief of some upholders of free enterprise, overproduction was not thought possible for years to come. This is, of course, provided that the world is to be properly fed. The C.C.F. wholeheartedly supports the' efforts of the food conference to lower trade barriers and to establish a permanent international organization on food and agriculture. Such an organization will have sufficient data, we hope, to plan scientifically to meet the worlds needs in an orderly way. Any other system permitting of disorganization such as we have seen in the past, when our grain elevators in western Canada were bursting with grain, while hundreds of thousands of people in our Canadian cities were going hungry and millions more were going hungry across the seas will only develop into a condition of trade rivalry and economic chaos.
I doubt that security for agriculture is attainable in Canada without the stability provided by external commitments, these arranged through international agreement. We welcome the government's efforts to obtain such agreements. But important as export markets are, the chief demand for farm products is here at home. The consumption of food stuffs has materially increased during the war years, and the reason is obvious to anyone. It is because people now receive more money with' which to buy these goods. Yet in spite of that, many of our people are still living without sufficient of these necessities of life.
Surveys show us that urban dwellers consume less than one pint of milk a day, that in forty per cent of our homes cheese is virtually unknown, and that if everyone had sufficient meat to eat we would consume in Canada more 
than three hundred million pounds of meat more than we do now. It is also interesting to note that three-quarters of our population eat less than one egg a day, the cheapest and most nutritive food we have. Let us then keep in mind this vast home market.
Everyone in this house will appreciate the need for social security measures so that the living standards of our people may be raised, and help provide healthful living for the children of these families. Besides, such measures will definitely increase the demand for farm products.
This group will continue to advocate research in the field of chemurgy. Dyson Carter, in his book "So Man May Prosper" states that one hundred American factories are utilizing the products of the farm to-day to produce synthetic materials. Oil, industrial alcohol, syrup, plastics, are produced in this manner. All of us know that during the great European war just concluded a large number of vehicles ran on rubber made from low-grade grains in urban factories. We are also advised that cotton is a synthetic product that can be made from low-grade grains. This should interest Canadians, who import each year large quantities of cotton for domestic consumption. The western members of the C.C.F. regret in this connection that no branch of the industrial development bank has been established on the prairies. Small industries dependent on raw materials from the farm must of necessity be established in western Canada if we are to stabilize western Canadian agriculture. Such industries would utilize any surplus which may accumulate and do much to balance western Canadian economy. They would also provide thousands of jobs for our young people, who now travel to distant parts of the land in search of work.
Reference is made in the speech from the throne to the government's policy of floors under farm products. Commendable as that may be, we in this corner of the house believe it would be much more satisfactory to establish basic parity prices for all farm products, these prices to bear a direct relationship to the cost of production-not a floor price but a price that varies with the changing cost of production and is related to the cost of goods which the farmer buys and uses.
Buying and equipping a farm costs a considerable sum of money, and operating costs vary little whether the crop be large or small. Canada has been protecting her manufacturing for quite some time. But no protection has been afforded agriculture except during war time. The agriculturists of this country have to compete in a world open market in

The Address-Mr. McKay
order to sell their goods. Protective tariffs have cost this country enormous sums of money. According to the late Hon. Norman Rogers, testifying before a royal commission dealing with the relationships of Nova Scotia with the rest of Canada, these are the actual figures: in 1931 Canadians paid $425 millions more than the world level of competitive prices to sustain their manufacturing plants. That amount was $40 per capita, or $200 per family of five persons, and whether or not a Liberal or a Conservative government has been at Ottawa has made little change in these schedules. Protection for manufacturing has increased our living costs, and if we can afford to do that for a secondary industry I insist that we should do the same thing for Canada's first industry, agriculture. The establishment of parity prices for farm produce commensurate with changing costs of production would do for the farmer what has been done in this country for the manufacturing interests for generations.
In addition to suggestions which I have offered, we of this group insist that better credit facilities be provided for the farming industry. In 1941 the "Canada Year Book" stated that forty-eight per cent of our owner-operated farms were mortgaged, and the average throughout Canada was $2,372 per farm. In the west the situation was even more serious. Credit unions have done us considerable service in western Canada and, I believe, in the province of Quebec, but this excellent cooperative enterprise, while it has rendered outstanding service, has its hands more or less tied. The C.C.F. has long advocated, and still continues to do, that an agricultural bank for western Canada and for eastern Canada be established in order that mortgages may be refinanced at 2J per cent interest. The government did establish an institution known as the industrial bank. It was apparently to assume the most risky and unprofitable post-war credit operations, namely the financing of small industry. Instead of bringing our credit system under social control, the government hopes that that institution will facilitate the construction of small industries which in pre-war days could not get credit. The efforts of this group at the time the industrial bank was set up to establish an agricultural institution of a similar kind fell on deaf ears.
Another part of our policy would be the appropriation of funds for water conservation and for irrigation of areas, particularly in western Canada, that are subject to drought. Such a programme would preserve our farms and at the same time would provide post-war employment. Projects of this kind in the United States have been particularly successful, and
we are informed by practical and experienced engineers that they are feasible on both the Saskatchewan and the Red Deer rivers. Definitely that programme will be a necessary part of our post-war industrial development, on which the Saskatchewan government has already embarked on a small scale.
In reference to crop insurance I should say this, that those crops, no matter whether they be in western or eastern Canada, which because of the nature of their production carry great risks, should definitely be protected. It is essential to the stability of agriculture. The present government's policy, implemented by the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, of providing a maximum of $2.50 an acre when the area is declared to be an emergency area owing to drought, is excellent as far as it goes, but I would suggest that that amount be increased from $2.50 an acre to $6 an acre and that payments be on an individual farm basis rather than on a township basis as is at present the case. The cost of such a programme could be calculated when computing the basic parity prices set for agricultural products.
Reference has been made in this house by several speakers to the income tax. I suggest that some consideration be given to the position of the farmer's wife who normally performs all the duties of an urban wife together with many heavy burdens of outdoor tasks. Frequently her labour saves the hiring of extra help which normally would be chargeable against the expense of operating the farm unit. I suggest that a further exemption be granted the farmer to take care of this situation.
Last, but not least, it would appear to a good many of us that farming conditions must be made more attractive if young people who are being discharged from our armed services are to return to the farms. While serving in the Royal Canadian Air Force as a personnel counsellor, in a period of three months I had 106 boys come to me who were formerly from farms. Of those 106 only twenty-three indicated any inclination to return to farm life. That seems a serious situation, but on inquiry the reason seemed obvious. Briefly, I will put it in this way. They have seen urban life, and they too vividly recall the days of distress they went through at the time of adolescence. Roughly speaking, only twenty per cent of our farm homes have electric current with which to do labour. Only one per cent of our farm homes have flush toilets. Only one farm in three has a telephone, and despite the need for transportation there is only one car to every two farmers.
I trust that in some small way I have shown the needs of agriculture and the urgency of
The Address-Mr. MacNicol

enriching prairie farm life. We can ill afford to neglect the people who till our soil. If that neglect persists the effect upon our national life may well be tragic. Goldsmith, in his "Deserted Village", depicts the consequences of a declining agriculture:
111 fares the land, to hastening ills a prey,
Where wealth accumulates, and men decay.
Mr. Speaker, I submit that the necessity should be recognized of Canada adopting an enlightened policy toward agriculture, a policy which not only will meet the needs of the farmer, but rehabilitate Canada's greatest industry.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been in this house for fifteen years-five years of that time on the government side and ten years on the opposition side of the house. During the last ten years I have been here, the work devolving on members of the official opposition has been strenuous, because until lately there were fewer than forty of us. But this session is altogether different. A large number of capable and brilliant men have been added to the Progressive Conservative ranks, and I wish to say a word of appreciation of those who have spoken on our side. I have not time to mention the new members who have spoken from the other parties, but a number of them have done very well also. On our side, however, the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Bracken) had held1 for a longer period than any other man the premiership in a British legislature. He has surely lived up to our fondest expectations and, in my judgment, has conducted himself on an eminent plane since coming here this session. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt), the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), the hon. member for London (Mr. Manross), the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy), all new members, have given addresses which have not been excelled by those of any other new members in my time during the past fifteen years. They will all add greatly not only to the strength of the opposition but to the debating powers of this parliament.
So far three ministers have spoken in this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I will not make any comment on the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). I will refer briefly to the remarks of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) and at greater length to the words of the bon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Howe). I simply 
wish to make an observation or two with reference to the remarks of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. I will tell him of something I heard on Sundaj^ last while on a visit to western Ontario. I heard this from a gentleman by whom I had the honour to be driven to a meeting which I was to address. He is quite well off and has two sons. Speaking about the family allowance, he said, "I am putting in the bank money sent me in the form of family allowance for my two sons for their future education in the event of its being required at some time. But I am wondering how it will help the education of the sons of the humble man, the son of the blacksmith, the machinist, the carpenter or any other artisan, and the humble farmer. I hope that if you have an opportunity you will mention this to the minister and suggest that he consider some means whereby something can be laid aside for the sons of those who are not as well privileged as my sons."
I thought that was a happy suggestion, because in my experience the sons and daughters of humbler people, wherever they have had a chance, have given a great account of themselves in this life.
This gentleman mentioned another matter with which I agree. It has to do with the soldier. In fact, I myself had a similar experience on Saturday last with a young soldier who is the counterpart of the one mentioned by my friend. This young man came to me on Saturday and seemed to be in distress. He said, "I have been six years overseas and hardly know what to do with myself. Everyone I speak to talks about something with which I am not familiar. They talk about baseball, golf, bridge, and one thing and another, whereas my last six years have been spent with guns, shells, cannon and bayonets. I cannot get my head down to thinking about a job." I suggest to the minister that in considering provision for returned soldiers special consideration be given these men; that the greatest sympathy be exercised and every effort made to get them back on their feet, and until they are back on their feet they should be taken care of in the manner in which soldiers who served four or five or six years, or less for that matter, should be cared for. That is all I have to say in reference to the remarks of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George.
With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Port Arthur, I shall have to disagree with some of the statements he made. The hon. member for Port Arthur, the Minister of Reconstruction, has a habit of making all-embracing statements. I have had long experience in employment. Not many in this

The Address-Mr. MacNicol
house have had more; perhaps none has had more and perhaps not many have had as much. So that I know something about employment. I was therefore surprised to hear the hon. member for Port Arthur, the Minister of Reconstruction, make the statement yesterday that at this moment two jobs are open for every applicant for a job. In my opinion that is absolutely impossible. I do not for a moment say that the minister was making a misstatement; he was just enthusiastic. It is not possible under normal circumstances, however, and much less under the present circumstances. There is no such thing as such a number of jobs going at the present time.
A little further the minister said that in 1946 we can expect an expansion of peacetime industry comparable with the expansion of industry generally during the war years.
I was in big industry during the last war; I was in big industry following that war, and again I say that statement cannot possibly be correct. I am not saying the minister intended to make an incorrect statement, but from my experience what he suggests is not possible. Everyone knows that, during this war, industry has been operating at many times the capacity it did during peace time. How, therefore, can the industrial fabric of Canada again in peace time take care of the number of positions which the minister has suggested in his statement? As I say, the minister is all-embracing in his statements about employment.
The brilliant young cartoonist of the Globe and Mail, of Toronto, Jack Boothe, on September 8 had a cartoon which in my opinion should attract the attention of the entire nation. The word "jobs" is perhaps the most important in the English language, and he emphasized this fact. He showed how allimportant it is at the present time. The cartoon, which was a classic, depicted jobs as monumental, gigantic and all-impressive; and they are. Anyone who has not a job or has been out of a job for any length of time knows how important it is to him to obtain one.
Two days later, to be exact, on September 10, backing up the cartoon of the young cartoonist, a large delegation of workers came here. They would not have come if the statement of the Minister of Reconstruction were correct, namely, that there are at present two jobs for everyone wanting a job. No; they came here because jobs are scarce and are getting scarcer. As every one knows who was there, they filled the railway committee room on that morning. Those who heard their remarks could realize their anxiety and their grave fears that the situation will become worse
and that more and more men will be laid off. I know that in my own constituency of Davenport, which has a large number of factories, some of which are large and some not so large, ever since the capitulation of Germany, and particularly since the capitulation of Japan, some factories have been laying off twenty hands, or perhaps a few dozen or a hundred or several hundred, and in one case a thousand or more. Now, that does not bear out the statement that there are two jobs for every one who wants one. My own experience, which has been gained from people coming to my door to get me to write letters for them to this place or that to get a job, is that the situation is not at all like that represented by the Minister of Reconstruction. I hope that he will not keep that frame of mind, but on the contrary that he and the government will do their utmost to organize and prepare in every possible way not two jobs for one but a job for every one, which will be amply satisfactory.
The minister also spoke about government plants. I presume he had in mind plants that the government had a lot to do with so far as their organization is concerned, wartime plants, and I intend to speak about two of them. I shall refer briefly to the Polymer plant at Sarnia. I spent quite some time in that plant, and having a knowledge of chemistry and engineering I could plainly see through all the various chemical operations that are carried out in that plant to produce the rubber.
In passing I wish to compliment all who have had anything to do with either the planning or organizing and completion of the Polymer plant. It is a credit to Canadian engineers and Canadians all round that they were able to build a plant to produce rubber in the satisfactory way in which the Polymer plant produces it. I am not going to take up the time of the house to say much about it, because there are other matters on which I wish to touch. The Polymer plant would be a subject for a forty-minute address in itself; but it was intensely interesting to watch the two different chemical reactions that produced the two different kinds of rubber, one kind for the tube and the other kind for the casing. On Sunday last I met a doctor at a memorial service I was attending. He had come over from that part of the province, and in the course of our conversation we talked about the Polymer plant. He told me that he had four tires which were made at Sarnia, that he has now driven them thirty thousand miles and that they have given him eminent satisfaction.

The Address-Mr. MacNicol
I suggest to the Minister of Reconstruction and to the government the imperative necessity of keeping the Polymer plant in operation in some way for the making of rubber if it is at all possible so to do. I hope the time has come when we Canadians can make at least some of the rubber we require. For the sake of trade perhaps we shall have to import some of it from outside Canada, but if the four thousand men and women now employed in the Polymer plant can be kept making rubber it will be an excellent thing for Canada. I hesitate to think what it would mean to the county of Lambton and the fine city of Sarnia if the Polymer plant ceased to make rubber. I suggest to the minister and to those associated with him, in view of the fact that the government has provided fifty million dollars to build and put that plant in operation as a war work, that if it is necessary to keep the plant in operation they allow whoever is operating it now or will be operating it in the future to use that capital investment on a long term and low interest rate. I would go so far as to suggest that the interest be not collected if that would keep the plant in operation. If it will keep four thousand men and women employed and give us our tires and rubber at the same price as that at which we can buy them elsewhere-and I am told they would be able to do that; I am not in favour of the Canadian people paying more for rubber than they can buy it for elsewhere -under those circumstances I am not opposed to the government letting the investment lie, not demanding the interest and not capitalizing the interest unless returns permit it.
I now wish to say a word or two about another great industry in a section of the country in which I spent some time this summer, namely, the lake St. John area in Quebec. The province of Quebec has a vast treasure in the lake St. John area. It is a fine agricultural section. I did) not know that before I went there. I had the idea it might be a barren, cold area, but I found it wholly the reverse. I found fine farms and prosperous farmers. So far as I could see, the whole area was ,a good agricultural area. It is an area that is rich in forest resources. There are a number of pulp and paper mills, such as at Jonquiere and Chicoutimi, and I have forgotten the names of the other places. It is a fine area both industrially and agriculturally. In the midst of it is that great lake, not so large as lakes go, but still a substantial lake of four hundred square miles area at the highest water level-not the normal but the level maintained by the dams at Isle Maligne. It is a beautiful picture. From the air the whole area looks like a flat bowl and in the

centre the lake. In fact the Indian name for lake St. John was Peguagomi, meaning "flat". We now call it by the beautiful name of lake St. John, from which runs a magnificent river. That river is not very long; I believe it ends about thirty miles south of the lake, because from there on while it is still called the Saguenay river it is really an arm of the sea, with the tide rising at the mouth of the river and going right up beyond Chicoutimi to the foot of the Shipshaw power plant discharge. In that thirty miles the water drops 320 feet.
Here is one of the most remarkable demonstrations of the ability of Canadian engineers, of whom I believe the principal one, whom I knew quite well, was the late Mr. H. G. Acres. His was the conception, I understand, of the final magnificent simplicity of that great power plant, which is almost inconceivable. I can picture how the first engineers, looking at the discharge at lake St. John (past) Isle Maligne and the other islands, watching the rushing waters go down Chute a Caron, must have been staggered by the magnitude of the task of harnessing that river; but thanks to the late Mr. Acres and those associated with him, whose names I cannot recall at the moment, this remarkable undertaking was carried out.
The first power plant is immediately south of the lake, at Isle Maligne, where there is a drop of 110 feet. From there down to the canal above Chute a Caron the water is level, because of the dams and two power plants at Shipshaw. At No. 1 plant the water drops 160 feet and at No. 2 plant it drops 210 feet. These power plants, taking water from the same canal, I believe represent the greatest concentration of power development at the present time in a single plant anywhere in the world. I am thoroughly conversant with Grand Coulee and Boulder dam, neither of which, so far as I know, is yet complete as to power installations. When Grand Coulee is completed it will be able to produce about
2.700.000	horse-power. Boulder dam when completed will produce about 1,835,000 horsepower. These three plants on the Saguenay river really are all one combined power plant, though the one at Isle Maligne is twenty miles up the river, since they all draw water from the same source. The day I was at Shipshaw the plant at Isle Maligne was producing
540.000	horse-power; No. I plant at Arvida, adjacent to Shipshaw and drawing from the same canal, was producing about 260,000 horse-power but could produce another 130,000, since they have the positions ready for the installation of two more generators, and at Shipshaw itself the production was
980.000	horse-power. I was surprised to find

The Address-Mr. MacNicol
that the name "Shipshaw" is just a name for the whole development. The Shipshaw river flows right in there at the very' place where the tide itself stops, and the first proposal was to deliver the water out of No. 2 plant into the Shipshaw river, which is immediately below it. But the engineers felt that the Shipshaw valley would not be large enough to take the water from that vast power plant, so they just turned the plant around and delivered the water into the Saguenay at the base of Chute a Caron falls, where the tide ceases. As I said, the day I was there No. 2 plant was producing 980,000 horse-power, so at that time the three plants were producing a total of something less than
1,800,000	horse-power; and that was not their full capacity. They could produce a great deal more than that. I believe if they added another storage reservoir to the three they now7 have they could raise their production to 2,500,000 horse-power, which would make this larger than any other plant in the world, barring Grand Coulee alone; and it may be some time before Grand Coulee produces anything like that.
The engineers deserve unstinted praise for what they have done. To have power of this kind it is necessary to have a continuous flow of a stated amount of water. I believe that with the reservoirs they have adjacent to the Saguenay river they can maintain a constant flow of 42,500 cubic feet per second. They are able to do this because away up the Peribonka river they built a large lake. That river was made famous by a noted writer, the author of Maria Chapdelaine, whose name I forget at the moment.

speechtext:
That river has on it a lake one hundred miles long, about what is called Passe Dangereuse; I suppose in English we would call it Dangerous Passage. The lake behind that dam contains a reservoir of 183 billion cubic feet of water in storage. Not far from that, on a stream which runs into the same river, they have created what they call lake Manouan, in which they have another 78 billion cubic feet of water in storage. In other words, on those two rivers or in those two reservoirs they have about 260 billion cubic feet of water in storage; and by raising lake St. John itself, with its own area when raised of 412 square miles, they are able to store another 170 billion cubic feet of water. So that they have behind their power plant an almost inexhaustible supply of water in storage.
Many times I have wondered what we are going to do to keep that vast power plant in operation after the war is over. If it can 47696-17
be so organized I believe that in this area, with the power available, we can locate enough industries to make up a large city, and still be able to send out to Quebec city and other cities in that vicinity such volumes of power as would make them all grow-because nothing in the world will make a city grow faster than cheap power. If that area is given the support it should be given, then I say that there is destined some time to be there a vast manufacturing industry.
At the present time, and I believe for some time to come, the aluminum plant at Arvida will use all the power available. The set-up of thaL plant is marvellous. I hold in my hand a piece of bauxite I took from one of the boats which come to Port Alfred. This is nonmetallic, but because it produces metal I should imagine it would be classified as a metallic ore. The bauxite is light enough, but we know that out of every ton of bauxite brought in from Demarara-British Guiana, half a ton of aluminum is manufactured. It is most interesting to watch a ship unloading bauxite, and later being loaded with paper from the Jonquiere paper mill, and from other paper plants in that area. After being loaded, the ship sails for England. Upon reaching there it is loaded with merchandise, and sent back to British Guiana. That is real trade! That is the kind of stuff to bring to Canada. Through the labour of about 8,000 men and women at the Arvida plant about half a million tons of aluminum is turned out each year.
May I say a word on behalf of the company operating at that point. It has built fine houses for its employees. A worker is permitted to buy his house at a low rate, I talked to several men and found them very happy in their employment at Arvida. The houses are heated and plumbed. Some of them are of stone, and all are beautiful. They range in size from four to six rooms, and I believe that about 1,800 have been built in that city. Arvida is a beautiful city, a credit to Canada, and particularly to the province of Quebec. The houses are rented at rates as low as S13.50 a month, running up to $34. That, indeed, is a low rental.
And that is the way it should be. A company of that description should go the limit- and, so far as I can see, it is doing so-to care for its employees. I believe it is taking the best of care, and is looking after the welfare of its employees. I, for one am going to urge as strongly as I can upon the minister in charge that if at some future time all the power there available cannot be used in the making of aluminum, some effort should be made to use it in the manufacturing of other commodities, so as to give employment to Canadians.

25S
The Address-Mr. MacNicol

Last night the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) spoke about the coming conference, and I believe other members of the government who have preceded him in the debate have made a similar reference. But we cannot be sure that the conference will be a success. I, for one, would ask that the ministers should not put all their eggs into one basket and base their hopes for employment upon something which may never materialize. The problem is too serious to neglect or to leave entirely to a conference.
I recommend that a careful survey be made of the report of the committee on reconstruction and rehabilitation which has met during the last three or four sessions of parliament, and over which at the last session the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) presided. That committee has tabled two excellent reports, to which reference was made yesterday by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). He was one of the most active members on the committee. He and I saw eye to eye on almost everything, with the exception of politics. When it came to jobs we were unanimous. The hon. member made reference to the work of that committee when he addressed the house yesterday, and had I the time I should like to do so to-day. However, I would point out briefly that no less than twenty splendid opportunities are set out in that report for the providing of jobs in a big way.
Every provision should be made to provide men with jobs, men from Toronto and elsewhere who are out of work. I say that projects should be ready to provide jobs. For instance, mention has been made about irrigation, one of my pet subjects. I am sorry to say that up to the present time very little can be done for Saskatchewan from the Saskatchewan river. Two or three years ago I recommended strongly in the house that the government should set up forthwith a Saskatchewan river authority, organized along the lines of the Tennesee valley authority, because that great Saskatchewan river runs through three provinces and should be given special attention. Certainly if all the water is taken out of it before it reaches Manitoba, then Manitoba will be left holding the bag.
Such an authority could state what volume of water should be taken from the river and at what points it should be taken. If such an authority were set up Saskatchewan should most assuredly receive from the South Saskatchewan river all the water required to irrigate west of Regina. This would mean the construction of large dams. But we are not ready to do that; why? Had I been the minister of the responsible department-and

perhaps I should not say this-I should have had) plans ready. I was a business man, and as such did things in a business way. Business men do not monkey-doodle and fiddle around, but go straight to work and do things.
Had I been minister I should have had ready at least the plans and specifications for the dams where required. Now look at the box we are in! While it may be said that nothing can be done for Saskatchewan, the same cannot be said about Alberta. We must do something. I ask the responsible minister to tell the house why he has not plans and specifications ready for the building of the Spring Coulee reservoir, which should and must be built, if we are to retain for Canada the water rights on the St. Mary river. Those plans should be ready.
I have surveyed the site carefully; I have made careful examinations there, and I know that the engineers have stated the position correctly. A dam can be built there and water can be conserved. Let me add that water is a most priceless heritage for the prairie provinces-and yet to-day we are letting billions and billions of cubic feet of it flow off down to Hudson bay, thereby making no return whatsoever to this country, when water required should be taken our of the river in Alberta- and might as well be, because in the states south of the boundary line they are taking it out, for purposes of irrigation.
The minister should be ready to send men at once to do that work. I would ask him this: What are the boys from the prairie provinces going to do when they come home? Last night he said:
Just as it took many months to move people from one locality to another into war jobs, it will take a shorter period to redistribute our people into peace-time jobs.
I presume a great many of the people who came from Saskatchewan to work in factories at Toronto, Stratford, Hamilton, Galt, Brants ford, and other eastern1 cities, will want to return to the west. What will there be for them to do? The minister should have his programme ready. Many are engineers. Many of them know something about the making and pouring of concrete, and how foundations should be set. The programme should be ready, so that those brave lads who rendered such high service on the plains of Europe, in the skies over Europe and on the seas, boys who had never seen ships or aircraft before they enlisted and were compelled to operate them, may have something to do when they return bo their homes.
Orders would soon be coming back to the factories in eastern Canada, and in that way

The Address-Mr. Maybank
men would be employed east and west. I would not hesitate to support a programme of 8100,000,000. What is $100,000,000?. It is hardly the price of a super-battleship, and nobody makes any fuss over the sinking of one battleship. But a programme of $100,000,000 would rehabilitate the whole of the three western provinces, particularly Saskatchewan and Alberta, and provide them with power and irrigation, and water for such fine cities as Regina and Moose Jaw, so that they could maintain their identity, and the power that would be developed would lead to the establishment of many industries in the western provinces. Irrigation now planned would put into productivity approximately 3,000,000 more acres of land. Look what that would mean all along the line, right down all the way from the irrigated area itself to eastern Canada. I have been out west many times, and my observation of all the towns and cities in the west has been that perhaps the city of Lethbridge is the finest example or at all events an extremely fine example of the prosperity which comes to a town or city in the centre of an irrigated area. The benefits flow all along the line from that thriving, prosperous and healthy city of Lethbridge.
In conclusion, may I say that I have deliberately refrained from saying anything of an acrimonious nature because from long association with workers and employees my heart goes out to them and I want to see them continued in employment and security. All of us together, every member of the house, should be devoting his time not to such debatable subjects-I mean in these times, perhaps I should call them educational subjects- as a new flag or a new anthem for Canada. Our minds should be concentrated on the production of jobs to take care of the thousands and thousands of our boys who are coming home and those thousands and thousands who are going to be thrown out of employment in this country.
It is all very nice for the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply to say: I can see one million jobs. Well, I cannot see them, and no other living man in this country can see them. A man came to me for a job some days ago and I told him, "I have just read that selective service state that there are 143,601 jobs vacant" -I am using just an arbitrary figure-"and there are only 31,275 applicants"-again an arbitrary figure. This unemployed man said to me, "The figures should be turned around the other way."
Last night the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply said something like this-and again 47696-17i
I am using arbitrary figures-that there are 232,601 jobs vacant and only 73,000 applicants. But you go to selective service for a job and what sort of job do they send you to? To a pick-and-shovel job or something of that sort. They are not sending men out to take a job as an engineer or machinist or as a chemist or other professional man. Oh, no; there are lots of so-called pick-and-shovel jobs, but not the kind1 of job a man wants to take who has a wife and family to keep and a home to maintain that he is purchasing. While on that subject I am going to suggest to the responsible minister that it is time that some plan be put into operation so that the unemployed worker will not, as he did during the depression, lose his equity in the house he is buying merely because he has lost his job and is unable through lack of earning power to keep up the principal and interest payments. Men are buying houses to-day at inflated prices, and they are inflated prices. A man that I know well boaight a house some days ago. I would not give $3,200 for it, and it cost him $7,800. He never will be able to pay for it. If he loses his job he may lose all his equity in the house. I hope that that will not be allowed to happen again. It was the most heart-breaking thing I saw during the depression. Yet I saw it happen to so many of our finest citizens, whole-souled, thorough Canadians, who had invested one or two or three thousand dollars in the purchase of a home which they would have been able to own some day had1 their jobs continued, but many of them, lost their jobs and, in due course, lost their equity Jn the homes they had been buying. It was one of the saddest things I have seen, and I hope that the government will take steps to see to it that workers unfortunate enough to lose their jobs do not also lose their equity in their homes, that at least they will get back the money they have put into the property.
