speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the last speaker (Mr. MacNicol). I think the whole house always enjoys hearing from the hon. member for Davenport. We always have an informative speech from him, and I know that so far as the members from western Canada are concerned they are glad to hear what he has to say because he shows that he is interested in problems right across Canada. Sometimes it has seemed, the problems of the prairies claim his special interest. When he presents a picture to us it is always clearly painted. I was disappointed for a little while this afternoon when he stayed away from the
The Address-Mr. Maybank

prairies for so long, for I feared that we were not going to hear from him to-day on our part of the world. But I was glad to see him come at last to the Saskatchewan river. I was reminded, as he spoke, of the old story of there being no mill by the dam site. We can only hope that he is wrong in his fear that irrigation will not soon be developed in the west.
In my first words, I wish to speak of two famous regiments. Reference was made to them yesterday by my colleague from Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch). Respecting these regiments I wish to make a suggestion, indeed a straight request of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Abbott).
The final turn of the scroll of the tragic drama that we call Hong Kong is being unwound, and the closing scenes bring some compensation for all the horror of that terrible episode. Equally those closing scenes remind us of the heroism of that episode. Greater even than the horror is the heroism. The final scene to-day shows that we have reunions in the city of Quebec, and reunions in my prairie city of Winnipeg. The Grenadiers will again meet their loved ones in my city, and the Royal Rifles of Canada will embrace their dear families in historic Quebec.
The whole picture as I review it leads me to make this specific request of the government through the Minister of National Defence. It is this, that in determining the composition of the permanent force of Canada for the future he will make sure that the identities of these two brave regiments will be maintained. It is my submission that the names of these heroic units should be kept in the Canadian army, before all the people, as a daily reminder to us of the imperishable deeds which are associated with their names.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South yesterday paid his respects to the new leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), and thanked him for getting out and giving him his house to live in. I wish to pay my respects to the leader of the opposition, he being for a long time a distinguished citizen of my province. I am sorry to see him in his present plight, but still, since he apparently desires it, I congratulate him upon the leadership of the Conservative party. That term "Conservative", I may say, comes most usually to my lips although I have no constitutional bias against using the expression "Progressive Conservative". I realize that nobody will be fooled by the prefix, so what does it matter?
Well, I congratulate him not merely upon leadership but upon the speech he made in this house a few days ago. It is not the first time I have heard the hon. gentleman

discourse. In fact I have heard him a number of times, and it has always been my view that he spoke with clarity and sometimes with the force of conviction. I feel that he is to be congratulated to-day upon his usual clarity.
I underscore at once that my congratulations are upon the form of the speech, not the subject matter.
Adding-to what I have said, I should like to review some of the leader's statements; and the first one to which I will refer commands my whole support. The hon. gentleman said as reported in Hansard at page 28:
I want to say, with all the emphasis at my command, that this nation will not stand for any chiseling down of the promises and commitments made to service personnel while they were fighting our wars abroad.
In these words the leader of the opposition was absolutely right, although why he should have adopted, as I thought, a minatory tone was rather hard to see. It must be admitted,
I think, that Canada has enacted already the best veteran legislation there is in the world. In spite of that, we all know there are still some blanks to be filled in and some improvements to be made. This must be done, and I do not think there is any disagreement about it.
Certainly the Canadian people are against "chiseling" in this matter; and I think that is why a great number of the Conservative old guard were left at home, because the electors remembered the chiseling operations of the Conservative government between 1930 and 1935, and they were not going to be fooled by the fact that the party had chosen a new leader and put a prefix to its name. However, the main point I wish to make is that we are all agreed that there must be no chiseling, that the administration of veterans' laws must be characterized by the utmost generosity.
I want now to offer a warning to the speaker whom I have quoted; I think it will not be out of place. I believe that he should tread warily in offering any criticisms of veterans' legislation. He should be careful not to suggest or seem to suggest that somebody else might do some chiseling. When he was premier of Manitoba he was the first person to take away a tax exemption which had been granted to veterans by the government which preceded him. But he who later admitted that he was "the most continuously successful political leader the British empire has produced in this century", was the first responsible statesman in this country to do a little chiseling on the veterans of the last war; and it is not likely to be forgotten.
I should like to make a further short analysis of the hon. gentleman's remarks.

The Address-Mr. Maybank
We all know that the opposition do not have to formulate policies when they are criticizing the policies of the government. Nevertheless it is not unreasonable to expect that a national figure will declare his belief or his disbelief on some points, or that there will be a positive assertion about something, to be found at some place in a speech which he makes. Now, perusal of his speech will reveal that never from start to finish did he declare himself as being favourable to an action or definitely against some action. There was only one exception; this was when, he said he was in favour of a reduction in the income tax. Of course everybody is in favour of a reduction in the income tax, nobody, probably, more profoundly or firmly than the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) himself. So that it is hardly worth while to give the leader o>f the opposition a score for that one positive statement of belief.
When the hon. gentleman dealt with meat rationing, for example-and this is illustrative of the whole thing-his unwillingness to commit himself was very noticeable indeed. He says, the people are asking so and so; the people are wondering what about this; they think such and such a thing ought to be done; they are going to be disappointed if so and so is not done. Never once did he state that he was against meat rationing; never once did he state that he was in favour of meat rationing. He says that if rationing is necessary it is due to some former fault of the government. Well, suppose that is admitted for illustration's sake. Even so, the situation has to be dealt with. If some sin of this administration in bygone days is the reason that meat rationing is necessary, still the problem is there, and he does not seem to be willing either to condemn or to approve.
Thinking over the whole speech, I was reminded of a poem of Kipling. I do not remember the name of the poem, but it was the story of a man who had died. He went to heaven seeking admission. Upon examination up there it was found that he had never done very much harm in his life, and prima facie it would appear that he was entitled to entrance; but on the other hand he had never done any good, and St. Peter slammed the door in his face. So he went down to the other place. But when he went down there the same sort of thing developed. St. Peter having thrown him from the one place, Nick interviewed him at the other; and sure enough he found he had never done much good and therefore he appeared to be entitled to admission to hell; but on the other hand there was no great evidence of depravity or wrongdoing in his life and Nick, being more robust in sin than usual that day, chased him off the premises of
hades and he was not admitted there. He was too neutral for either place. I do not remember just what did become of the soul after that; he moved back and forth, I think, between the two stations. While I cannot say for certain the subsequent facts, it has occurred *to me that perhaps there is something in the doctrine of reincarnation. This neutral soul perhaps entered the body of another person, or if that be not so, he will yet do so and will be back in this life before long. If already back, I presume he has already been chosen as leader of the Conservative party, and if he is not already reincarnated I expect that before long he will be chosen as leader of that party when in a couple of years' time they are shopping around again to get another leader. In a couple of years they will have to have some person else to carry their burnt-out torch.
I do not wish to emulate the leader of the opposition by leaving any uncertainty as to my views on the subject of meat rationing. I do not believe in pussy-footing about it. I recall that Jesius spoke with approval of those who had fed other people who were hungry and who had clothed other people who were naked. I know of no better doctrine than that, and it directs me to support the plans of to-day. I know there may be a difference as between the Christian concept of charity and the aim of serving our own convenience, but in any such case I am going to be guided by the. former and not the latter consideration. I wish to add, although I think it unnecessary, that if any economic justification is needed you will find it in this, that the wheat we already sent to Greece will pay dividends to us and to our children, great fat dividends, for many years to come.
If we are to feed the hungry we shall have to see that there is fair play with regard to the remaining food in this country. We cannot just leave it to be purchased by the more well to do in the community. We have to have some plan for dividing it up. That means rationing.
I think it is probable some changes will be found necessary in the plans at the present moment. It would be an odd thing if such were not, the case. But the need of rationing, when you have induced scarcity, surely must be apparent to all. There may be quarrelling about some detail or another, but if we are to feed the hungry we must have a plan of division for that part which is left. I believe that after what I have said no one will be in any doubt as to my view. Whether my stand will be satisfactory to all or most, I do not know, but 1 do not want anyone to be in doubt as to where I stand on this matter.
The Address-Mr. Maybank

One of the troubles of the Minister of Finance is that people ask for tax reductions and also ask for expenditures. I am>
afraid I would have to plead guilty if a charge of that kind were made against me. However, the expenditure I wish to recommend to the government is an urgent one, and on the other hand I believe it is not a large one.
What I wish to recommend is that the insurance principle with relation to pensions should be extended to those of the forces who have seen Canadian service. I have already met with a considerable number of cases of injustice where veterans who, through no fault of their own-and mark that, that is one important point I would put forward-did not have overseas experience, and are disabled, which almost certainly would not have been the case if they had not been in the forces. Worse still, there have been cases of death and widows are without pensions by reason of the law as it stands to-day. It seems to me that the extension of the insurance principle is a most important piece of legislation.
Moreover, the cost of this can now be seen. It could not be seen in 1940. It will not all come at one time. It extends over a period of time, and I believe it is absolutely necessary in the circumstances to-day.
About the reduction in taxation, as I said, everyone is in favour of it. I have been satisfied all along that every possible reduction in direct taxes would be made. I have a feeling that the Minister of Finance cannot do as much in 1945, when the budget comes down so late in the year, as can be done next year, but I feel sure that the government is well seized of the fact that we cannot have a satisfactory reconversion, a reconstruction; we cannot have a recreation of productive life and consequent employment unless there is a substantial reduction in rates.
I hope that indirect taxes will not be overlooked. They press most heavily upon those who are least able to pay. Indirect taxes pyramided on top of one another result in a great increase in the final cost of the articles people use. A friend of mine had to get two chains for his bicycle in the United States. The cost was $6, and by the time he got them it was $10. Shotgun shells and other types of ammunition are prohibited from import by reason of indirect taxes. I am not suggesting that the articles I have mentioned are weighted heavily in the cost of living chart or schedule. But they illustrate facts covering a very long list of articles that people have to buy and that figure often quite importantly in the cost of living and increase it greatly.
(Mr. Maybaiik.J
Another thing about indirect taxes-and this applies particularly to tariff taxes-is that the government often does not get the tax anyway. It very often goes to some local manufacturer instead of going to the government.
Since I have said a word about both expenditures and taxation, I should like to make a suggestion tending to harmonize the two apparently conflicting ideas. It is this. Search for waste and unnecessary expenditure, and be vigilant in searching. There must have been lots of waste during the war and I do not think anyone is very critical about it. When a six thousand million dollar business or machine is quickly developed and is made to function it is inevitable that there must be a great deal of waste, particularly when the purpose of the machine is to save the liberties of people. People are not going to be too finicky about the careful conservation of a dollar in these circumstances. The situation has changed now, however, and I submit that economy should be the order of the day from now on.
Here is an example of waste. John Doe is going to be discharged from the air force. He is located at Saint John and is on furlough in Winnipeg. He is going to be discharged; that is decided. Why should he not be discharged from Winnipeg? No; it cannot be done. He has to go to Saint John, the reason given being that he has to turn in his equipment. No business concern would operate in that way. There is no business man in the world who would put himself to the expense of bringing a man back from Winnipeg to discharge him in Saint John in order to give him signature for some articles he has in his possession. Of course, expenses have to be paid both ways, from Winnipeg to Saint John and back again; and other expenses besides travelling expenses are paid. In addition you have a loss to the community of that man, who is not engaged in the .production of wealth when he could be. I believe such acts can be carried out more expeditiously and cheaply. Economy should be the order of the day. I Know that officers who are making rules will impose all kinds of objections, but when officers are told that such and such a thing must result, it generally results. As a matter of fact, in the particular case I have mentioned, if all the equipment that John Doe had were lost it would not add up to as much as it cost to take him to Saint John and back to Winnipeg again.
Finally, I wish to say how much I welcome the policy of the government, as evidenced in the speech from the throne, of the recognition of a growing spirit of Canadianism in the country. For a great many years it has irked

The Address-Mr. May bank
me that if I said I was a Canadian my assertion could not end there. In effect it was claimed that there was no such thing as a Canadian. Like millions of others I thought and spoke and felt and acted1 like a Canadian, but I imagine I was not one because there was no such thing. This people within the bounds of what is called Canada-there cannot be any argument about the name of the territory-is great enough to declare that there is such a thing as a Canadian, and the world will certainly respect it. Our stature in the eyes of the world is greater than it has ever been before, and it has grown apace in the last few years. I welcome particularly the legislation that is forecast, which is thus a recognition of Canadianism, the law respecting citizenship, the law adopting a national flag of suitable design and the law adopting a national anthem.
There is another step we should take. We should devise a method for ourselves of amending our constitution, and we should do it soon. We could have done this long ago but we gave preference to other things. Not merely is it inconsistent with our own dignity as a nation to leave matters as they are, but it is putting an improper onus upon the parliament at Westminster. We have been and are treating the British parliament like a chore boy. Moreover, there may some day be an application for a constitutional amendment in the manner that we have so far been following which will be a highly contentious matter; the parliament over there or the government of the day over there will be placed in a highly embarrassing position in being required to decide between two contending factions in Canada, and we have no right to impose that burden. We should make sure that it will never occur; we should make sure by taking into our own hands the power of amending the constitution.
I am not at the moment going to suggest what formula we might adopt. Some sections of the constitution might be amended by the mere passing of resolutions in these houses of parliament; resting a certain period of time on the table, as the expression is, and no objection being taken, they would then constitute amendments. That would apply only to minor matters. On the other hand, it may be that we would have to work out some voting method-I think that is the most likely plan to be acceptable-such as they have in the United States and in all federal countries. The late Ernest Lapointe at one time spoke with approval of a plan, namely, that if two-thirds of the provinces advocated a change
in constitution, that would effect the change, provided that it did not impinge upon racial and religious rights, and if such rights were touched, then unanimity of the provinces would be necessary. That plan would probably be acceptable across Canada. I am not advocating it especially, but it is one of the plans that could be considered as soon as we decide that we shall take the constitution into our own hands. All I wish to urge to-day is that we must turn our attention to becoming masters of our own constitutional law. From that much more can follow in the way of progress and improvement.
As a footnote I should like to point out to you, sir that the various interprovincial conferences we have been having these last few years have been adopted really as a cumbrous substitute for constitutional amendment. Of course that is a dangerous and unsatisfactory method of getting along in this country. As all hon. members know, as the situation now stands, practically any person out of ten people can upset any possibility of agreement. Remember what happened a few years ago. Three men did not wish to sit in a conference; result, no agreement. Over the last several years this government by dint of tremendous work has overcome to a certain extent the difficulties that have resulted from the breaking up of that interprovincial conference. It has been a heavy task, and we cannot hope to carry on our governmental business in this country by various makeshift agreements, one following upon the other. We cannot run the risk of progress being held up by one, two or three wilful men.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to just about all of the speeches which have been made thus far in this debate. I would say as a general comment that there is complete unanimity in all parts of this house in the expression of the desire for a better Canada. I would say, however, that there is not the same unanimity as to what constitutes a better Canada. Certainly I do not consider that some of the
The Address-Mr. Kuhl

policies which have been advocated thus far, if applied to our nation, would make Canada a better nation. Furthermore, I believe there is also a lack of complete unanimity as to the means to be employed to bring about a better Canada.
Mention has been made by a few of the hon. members who have thus far spoken of the fact that we have not yet established a national objective. It has been suggested that before we can proceed logically we must lay down some fundamental objective to attempt to attain in the future. Personally I recognize that we must pass through a period of transition, and that during the period of reconversion we cannot hope for the things we may expect later on. Nevertheless I believe we should certainly indicate what we consider to be the long range objectives we are hoping to achieve, and do all in our power to implement them gradually as we pass through this period.
What is the objective that has been enunciated more frequently than any other thus far in this debate? I would say that with the exception of the members of the Social Credit group each hon. member in turn has enunciated an objective which I consider to be both impossible and undesirable. What is that objective? It has been proclaimed on the hustings as well as here in the house. Each individual member, in monotonous repetition, has proclaimed that the thing we must have abqve all else in this country is full employment. Hon. members have been talking about a new order, a new way of life and a new outlook. Well, I beg to ask: what is new about full employment? Work is the oldest thing in the world; it is as old as Methuselah. Most hon. members may have been elected on a programme of full employment, but I can assert that I was not. As I listened to radio broadcasts and such public speakers as I had the opportunity to hear, invariably they said, "Elect me and I will put you to work." Personally I did no such thing; I told my electors that if they saw fit to reelect me I would do everything humanly possible to put everybody out of work, and I think I spoke to as great a cross-section of the electors of my constituency as most hon. members did. 1 addressed no fewer than forty-nine public meetings during the campaign; I do not know whether any hon. gentleman here did better than that. But I can say that on' every occasion I made the same statement, and the electors of Jasper-Edson saw fit to reelect me as their spokesman in the House of Commons for the third consecutive time with a greater majority than ever before.
I have already asked the question: what is there new about work? If all we want out
[Mr. Kuhl 1
of this life is full employment and a job, why did we ever dispose of Adolf Hitler, who was the greatest provider of work the world has ever seen? He could create more jobs in one day than the Prime Minister of this country could create in his lifetime. Not only did he put all Germany to work; he put all Europe and eventually the whole world to work. I say that at least as far as my constituents are concerned, they are looking for a holiday. Some of them have worked for one hundred years and have not had a holiday yet. I should like to suggest as an antidote to the phrase "full employment," the slogan "full enjoyment."
As I have said already, I believe those elected on the platform of full employment have been returned on a programme which is impossible as well as undesirable. Why do I say it is impossible? As I listen to hon. members take part in this discussion, I am amazed. One would think we were still living in the oxcart days, when people made their living with their bare hands. Every hon. member, whether he is an industrialist, a professional man, a farmer or whatever he may be, must know we are living in the greatest age of machine power and mass production methods man has ever seen. Everywhere you go in industry to-day, whether into a manufacturing plant, a mine, or on a farm, you see one man with one machine doing the work of hundreds or perhaps thousands of people. Jusl consider the position during the war. We had approximately two million of our ablest producers out of work, as far as the production of the essentials of life was concerned. They were not producing those things which would have enriched our lives; they were producing things which were destroyed and wiped out of existence. Yet with those two million of our best producers out of production the rest of us carried on and provided all the essentials for ourselves and for them as well, on a grander scale than has been enjoyed by most people in the last fifteen or twenty years. Surely this indicates that there has entered into our national life a factor the like of which has never before been witnessed in the history of mankind; that is the power machine. No doubt yesterday hon. members received in their mail, as I did, copies of a publication entitled "Timber." I should like to draw to their attention-probably they noticed it, but did not get the full significance of it-the illustration on t-he first page of this publication. It seems to me particularly applicable at this time, inasmuch as a great deal of the discussion in the debate has centred around housing.

The Address-Mr. Kuhl
On this page I find two illustrations of lumber-piling machinery, and under one of those illustrations I find this statement:
Paul Bunyan, the legendary Hercules of the woods, was just a piker! Here's a man equipped to lift up to 15.000 pounds of lumber to a height of 171 feet from bottom of load to ground. He can trundle that load around the yards at speeds up to 35 miles per hour and manoeuvre like a jack rabbit.
Then the descriptive material in respect of the second illustration, which shows a lumbercarrying machine, is as follows:
Or take the lad in photo B. He straddles 6 tons of lumber, picks it up and rolls away with no more muscular exertion than Paul Bunyan selecting a toothpick.
This publication came into the hands of hon. members only yesterday. I point out, however, that probably they do not get the significance of what is involved in these illustrations.
Turning to a later page in the magazine, I find an illustration of a chain saw, and the following advertising material:
A well deserved tribute, for its speed in felling and bucking is almost uncanny .	.	.
enabling one crew to do the work of 20 men using cross-cut saws.
Those are only a few of the illustrations 1 chanced upon in looking through this publication. In addresses I have had the privilege of making in this chamber I have placed on record page after page of statistics indicating the extent to which the modern power machine has displaced human effort. I shall not worry the house on this occasion by repeating what I have said earlier. However, I think every hon. member must be aware of the fact indicated by these illustrations, because time and again they have seen the actual machinery in operation. These labour saving devices are typical of every industry, including farming. To-day one man and his son can accomplish on a farm what it required crews to accomplish only a few years ago.
The same is true throughout all industry. I ask, in all sincerity: How can hon. members suggest logically that we can have jobs for everyone who is willing and able to work, in the face of such circumstances. They must realize that there are only so many hours of work to be done. Regardless of what is to be produced, only so many hours of work are required for that production. If it takes four hours to produce a certain unit, how can anyone insist logically that it must take eight? Yet that is what hon. members are implying when they are insisting that we must have full employment.
I have heard it argued before and probably before the conclusion of this debate it will be argued again, that machines make more rather 47696-18
than less work. About the only come-back ever made to me in respect of machines displacing human labour was that of an hon. member who pointed out on one occasion that someone has to make the machines. Well, for goodness' sake, are the machines made with bare hands? No; machines are made with machines.
To-day employment has become largely that of button pressing and lever pulling. During the war I had the pleasure of going through a number of industrial institutions, and I can say that most of the work boils down to just *that.
I have before me some statistics indicating the truth of the assertion that the necessary number of hours of work is constantly decreasing. and that machines are putting men out of work. These figures are taken from a United States publication entitled "Man-hours and Distribution," and I refer particularly to a table taken from a study entitled "Machinery, Employment and Purchasing Power" made by the national industrial conference board in the United States.
This publication gives statistics in respect of the number of hours of work and the material produced over a period of years in the United States. The figures show that at the turn of the century, 1900, the number of man hours per unit of production for all industry in the United States stood at 6-3. Then, leaving out the intervening years, we find that for 1935 the figure under the same heading is 2-31. Does this not indicate that the use of machines is having the effect of decreasing the number of hours of necessary work?
It will be noted that the last figure set out in the table is for 1935. While I have no figures for 1945, I should not be the least bit surprised if the figures stood at about one man hour per unit of production. These figures show that to-day with the use of machinery it is possible to produce in one hour about six times the quantity produced in the same time at the turn of the century. Or, to put it another way, to produce an article today only one-sixth of the time is required that was required at the turn of the century.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was endeavouring to establish that the future welfare of Canada must be predicated upon a sound objective, and I had indicated that the objective which was being proclaimed by most hon. members was that of full employment. I challenge that objective as being either sound or desirable. I think we have not yet decided in this house or in this country whether full employment is a means to an end or an end in itself. As I listen to hon. members discussing the subject in the house I find them constantly confusing the two. I have not heard anyone yet clearly and distinctly indicate whether he believes in full employment as an end in itself or merely as a means to an end, and I think it ought to be made definitely clear by every hon. member who speaks on this subject. So far as I am personally concerned I consider that full employment is not an end in itself, but a means to an end, and it should never be regarded as anything else.
From time to time in this house hon. gentlemen, including such members as the member for Davenport, (Mr. MacNieol) who spoke this afternoon and others, arise and indicate the tremendous number of public works projects of one kind and another that are feasible and desirable in this country. I commend them for all these suggestions, and in particular the hon. member for Davenport,

who has rendered valuable service to this house for the work he has done in that regard. But the question I wish to ask him is: What is his objective in all of these suggestions? Is his objective the schemes he has in mind, or is it that of merely providing jobs for people? Do we want to build roads to put people to work or because we want roads? Do we want to build bridges to put people to work or because we need bridges? Do we want to build homes to put people to work or do we want homes in which people can live? I suggest that the only logical and sensible attitude to take is to build roads, homes, bridges, schools and hospitals for the sake of the object itself which is being built, and not merely for the sake of giving work. If all these projects can be carried out by a few individuals sitting in their offices and pulling levers and pushing buttons, then let it be done in that way. That is just about the stage we have reached at the moment in our production system.
I have asked on previous occasions-and I do so again and shall continue to do so just as long as this subject is discussed in the manner it has been-hon. members when they rise in their places and discuss full employment to define that term which they use. I think much of our discussion is fruitless largely because we do not define our terms. We debate and discuss subjects and each of us has a different definition of the terms we are using. I would ask those who assert that we must have full employment, what have they in their minds as to what constitutes full employment? The general term used is a job for everybody who is willing and able to work. What does that mean? Does it mean that there is available or can be made available an eight-hour day for everyone from sixteen to sixty years of age? Or what does it mean? I shall not dwell on this angle much longer. But I wish to indicate that for my part I consider full employment is only that work which the power machine cannot do. I consider that sound and sensible and logical, and if it is not, I want to be told why it is not. Is that the definition which hon. members have in mind when they speak of full employment?
I have pointed out in times past, and supported it with statistics, that if in this day and age we use machine power to the maximum possibility'-this was true before the war and it is certainly more so since the war-the manhours of work necessary to produce the highest possible standards of living in this nation need be very few. I indicated by statistics that an income of over four thousand dollars' worth of consumable goods for every family of four in

The Address-Mr. Kuhl
this nation could be produced with no more necessary hours of work than four hours a day four days a week by those between the ages of twenty-five and forty-five. I am not going to take the time to produce that evidence which I gave to the house on a previous occasion. I simply mention it now to indicate a different angle to the subject from that which has been discussed so far in the house in this debate.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The Liberals and Conservatives in this house have been championing the cause of private enterprise. I wish to do so too, because as a Social Crediter I believe in private enterprise. But I believe that the Liberals and Conservatives have unknowingly done private enterprise a great deal of harm by reason of the fact that they attribute a responsibility to private enterprise which is not a responsibility of private enterprise, and by so doing they leave themselves open to a first-class charge by the socialists and the communists. They assume that it is the duty and the responsibility of private enterprise to provide jobs and employment. They assume that responsibility on behalf of private enterprise, and then the socialists come along and say, Well, you had ten years before the war to prove it, and you did not do it; there was more unemployment than ever before in the history of the nation. And what come-back have the Liberals and Conservatives? Well, they have not any, but they should have, and the only way they can have a come-back is by denying responsibility for full employment. Speaking on behalf of private enterprise, I deny that it has any responsibility to provide jobs for anyone. That is not the purpose of private enterprise. I would ask hon. gentlemen of the C.C.F. who have businesses of their own, those who have farms, do they hire men on the farm when they do not need them? Do they hire them for the fun of it? No, they hire men only when they need them, and when they are through with them they dismiss them.

speechtext: We must reconcile ourselves to two conditions. The first is that we are faced with an ever-decreasing number of manhours of work. I granted in my preliminary remarks that in a period of readjustment we probably cannot hope to achieve what we should as a long-range objective, but I believe we are here laying down long-range objectives, as well as policies for the immediate future, and I repeat that we must reconcile ourselves, because we are in a power machine and mass production age, to an ever decreasing number of man-hours of work.

Another thing to which we must reconcile ourselves is a new source of income. The concern which I have for the people whom I am privileged to represent is not that they shall have jobs but that they shall have incomes, and that is a vastly different thing.

The reason we must reconcile ourselves to that fact is quite obvious. If one machine displaces 100 or 500 or 1,000 men it is obvious to anyone that it also displaces the pay cheque. But the goods go on piling up; the prices are still on them, but the people have not incomes with which to purchase those goods.
The first thing we must do is to set up a national balance sheet. As a nation we have never done that. We must discover what we have in real wealth on the one hand and what purchasing power the people have on the other, and compare the two, and I am satisfied we shall find that the people are short just about forty to fifty cents on the dollar. I have not time to attempt to prove that, but as time goes on during this session we of the Social Credit group are certainly going to elaborate on that aspect of our policy. I grant that if that premise is destroyed the basis of the whole Social Credit proposals ceases to exist, but I am satisfied that it cannot be disproved. What we are suffering from and will suffer from more and more as time goes along is an actual physical shortage
The Address-Mr. Kuhl

of purchasing power, and not a maldistribution. We hear a lot, particularly from the socialists, about a redistribution of profits. I challenge them to redistribute all the profits and they will still be short of money to distribute the goods. The greatest false assumption which is made in economic thinking is, that for every dollar's worth of goods there is somewhere a dollar in money, and that if you divide up the money you are automatically dividing up the goods. The conclusion would be true if the premise were correct, but the premise is not correct.
So we must reconcile ourselves to a new source of purchasing power. No adjustment of wages or prices either to the primary producer or to the secondary producer can effect a cure. There must be a source of income outside of wages and outside of prices, and that source of income must arise through the national bank of Canada. National money must be issued to the people direct in the amount of the deficiency which exists between total production and total buying power. The issuance of national money direct to consumers in this fashion is not something for nothing. When the government through its national bank issues purchasing power direct to consumers it is doing nothing more or less than monetizing the wealth which already exists, which has been produced and belongs to the people, but which they cannot acquire because there is no money anywhere in existence with which to buy it.
I shall not have sufficient time on this occasion to develop fully the thought which I have introduced. There is one other important point I should like to make before I resume my seat.
Most of the discussion which has taken place thus far has centred around providing or enabling the people to enjoy security. Each member in turn has indicated how he believes the people should be enabled to become secure, but how much have we had said about the freedom of the individual? How many hon. members have dwelt at any length on the freedom of the individual? I thought that was largely what we fought this war for. I should like to hear hon. members define freedom. What is freedom? When is a man free and when is he not free? If one may judge from the remarks of some hon. members it seems that all that is involved in freedom, as far a3 they are concerned, is a full belly and a warm back. I consider that there is more to freedom than that. That is the freedom of a slave. I consider that no one has freedom unless he has the freedom of choice, as was indicated by my colleague the hon. member for Edmonton East. Freedom of choice means

freedom to choose or to refuse one thing at a time. Canadians will never have freedom of choice until they are first secure. They must be enabled to enjoy their heritage, which is substantial, whether they work or whether they do not. In addition to that, they must have the right to add to their purchasing power by securing the necessary work of their choice.
A few government supporters have pleaded for patience with the government on the part of opposition members. I am willing to be patient for legitimate reasons. I grant that there are physical limitations which it is impossible to overcome; but as I listened to some of the ministers, notably the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Claxton), I detected' something that I suspected I would be hearing before long. He said something about creating appetites which could not be satisfied. It will not be very long before I expect to hear members of the government side, each in turn, saying that we cannot do this and cannot do that because we have not the money. To establish a new order it is not necessary to throw out the whole of the old. Let us preserve the best in the old order, remove the abuses and take care of the deficiencies and it will work to perfection.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate you on your elevation to the high office you hold. I am sure you will fill it with distinction to the house as well as to yourself. I am one of the many new members who have come to the house this year and I have enjoyed the wonderful addresses made by different members. It has indeed been a treat. I have also enjoyed the barbs of sarcasm that have been good-naturedly leveled by each side. Especially do I remember the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), addressed to our side of the house, that we were unfortunate enough to come in third position on the soldier's vote. This reminds me of my boy coming running to me when he thought I had done something wonderful, "Daddy, daddy, how did you do it?" 'But that is the way with children.
To-day in my mail I have twelve letters which I have received from butchers and meat-merchants in my riding and none of them is praying for the government to retain the controls on the rationing of meat. To some of these men the loss is largely in cooked meats. If you take this list and add it up you will see that they have lost in the past few weeks possibly 3.000 pounds of cooked meats, and some of the butchers say they will not continue in business. One of them says it is impossible

The Address-Mr. Menary
for him to do the work he has to do. He serves his customers, and it takes him so long to explain the rationing system, and the bookkeeping afterwards again takes up so much time that he cannot do the work.
I am sure that all citizens of Canada are willing to help the mother country. We have plenty of cattle to do this and after that commitment is filled we have enough for ourselves. There are great herds of cattle in my riding. I can name three farmers within, a radius of four or five miles of my local town. One farmer has 100 large steers weighing around 1,300 pounds each; another farmer, his neighbour across the road, has about sixty steers and forty head of dairy cattle; and a third farmer-I will mention his name, Frank Gamble-has 325 head of cattle on the grass. There does not seem to be a scarcity of cattle but we want a market.
This is common throughout my riding, and I may say that last week there was a load of cattle returned from the stockyards to that part of the country because of the glut caused by bad marketing. There is no shortage of cattle. Take the statistics for 1944 and look at the marketings of different stockyards across Canada. For the first thirty-seven weeks of
1944	there were 933,736 head of cattle marketed, and for the first thirty-seven weeks of
1945	there were marketed 1,168,157. That does not show any scarcity of cattle.
In my opinion the government should remove these controls because, as I have said, we have an ample supply of cattle to fill our commitments to the mother country and after that is done we can open the gates to the United States. We do not want a continuance of the stockyards being glutted with stock with the result that prices fall and farmers lose money. A farmer takes in his cattle expecting to receive 11, Hi or 12 cents and after keeping them for a week he sells them at 10i cents. I know a farmer in our district who took ten head of cattle to the union stockyards. He sold nine head, and one bullock was left for two weeks and finally died. This man could not get any insurance and he had a loss of over $100.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) last week mentioned something about the weighing of cattle at the stockyards. He stated that the capacity for weighing was only 4,000 cattle a day. As we are conversant with stockyards and have sold many thousand of dollars worth of produce to them, I would say that this could easily vary. For instance, if they weighed these cattle by the carload I am sure they could weigh 10,000 head of cattle in one
day; but if they have to weigh them by one or two to a lot, or two or three, it takes up more time.
They have four scales in operation at the stockyards and I do not think the trouble is in the matter of weighing. It is a matter of the packers going into the country and buying cattle and shipping them into their own yards and to the stockyards and the public are not aware of this fact. This condition can only be corrected by the government under their emergency powers.
The people of Canada to-day want to do everything possible to help to feed the multitude of people who are starving in Europe and who have suffered so much in this terrible struggle. I believe that all parties in this house desire to see this accomplished. To-day we are witnessing in Canada and throughout the continent one of the biggest strikes in history. I believe that the great trouble of this mass unemployment in the big cities is partly owing to living conditions. There are no gardens, no lawns, no playgrounds for the children. I have always believed and advocated that no city should grow over a hundred thousand in population and that manufacturers should spread their manufacturing plants over the rural sections where certain parts could be manufactured and shipped into a central point to be assembled. In that way the labouring man could have an acre or half an acre of ground and could keep some hens, a cow or something like that. In that way he would be a more satisfied man and the farmer would also have a market for his products nearer to his home.
I wish to speak on the income tax. I should like to say a few words here in regard to the farmer's income tax. As a farmer I know something of the difficulties of the farmer, the poor remuneration he receives for his work, and so forth. He possibly works longer hours and has less opportunity to take a vacation than individuals in any other occupation. He can do his best in cultivating the soil and planting his seed, but he has no control over the rainfall or the dry weather, or the pests that prey on his crop. He suffers more than anyone else from extreme variations in prices. When he has a large crop there is usually a lowering of the price level. If he has a poor crop he gets probably a higher price but he may have very little to sell. His only opportunity to make any money is when he happens to have a good crop and there is failure in other districts. His average earnings over a period of years are only very moderate, and therefore it is unfair to have to pay income
The Address-Mr. Menary

tax on the years when he has a fair return unless the years of poor return are taken into consideration-.
I think it would' appeal to everj'one, and all fair-minded persons would agree that the ordinary farmer should get some redress as to his income tax, because in the good years he pays out and in the bad years he gets no rebate. Probably in, no other business do values fluctuate so radically as in the case of the farmer. The ordinary farmer with a hundred acres or less should not have to file an income tax return as far as his farming operations are concerned, if he is solely engaged in farming.
I should like to say a few words about the adoption of a new flag for Canada. My riding views with alarm the matter of a new flag and a new national anthem. I represent a great constituency which has sent overseas over one thousand boys, many of whom have not returned to the families who loved them.. We offer our deepest sympathy to them. These boys went to fight that we might in the future be saved the horrors of war that other nations have suffered, and more especially the continuous bombing, the restrictions on food1, clothing, housing and other necessities which have been the lot of our mother country and during which they have shown such wondrous endurance. This has awakened our sympathies and admiration for these brave people. We cannot forget the great work of the British navy or the great fight put up by her soldiers, assisted by soldiers of the British commonwealth, in North Africa, Sicily, Italy, France, Holland	and	Germany;	and	I am
sure my constituents will not be satisfied with any flag that does not display as a most important part of its design the old union jack which has braved a thousand years the battle and the breeze, and which throughout the past through all the world has stood for bravery, integrity and fairness of the British people.
Mr. STANLEY KNOWLES	(Winnipeg
North Centre):	Mr.	Speaker,	like	otherhon. members	from	Winnipeg	who	have
spoken in this debate, I should like in my first words to give expression to the deep sense of gratitude that is felt in our city over the release from imprisonment of those heroic Canadians who fought at Hong Kong, including the Winnipeg Grenadiers. As has been said already by others who have preceded me, the fact that people in Winnipeg are now receiving messages from their loved ones, the fact that some of these men are already arriving home, has touched the heartstrings of the people of our city in a way we can all understand.

I have looked over the lists of the men who have been freed as they have appeared in our Winnipeg papers these past few days, and I have been struck once again by the large number of the men in the Winnipeg Grenadiers who came from the constituency I have the honour to represent. I cannot forget that many of these young men, enlisting as they did in the early months of the war-many of them went to Jamaica before they went to Hong Kong-are young men from homes that experienced the deepest bitterness of the depression this country went through in the 1930's. Nevertheless these young men were prepared to do their part, and I trust that this parliament will take a solemn vow that they must never again return to the conditions they and their families went through in those tragic thirties.
I wish to join with those who have urged the government to make suitable recognition of the experience through which these Hong Kong heroes have gone. I support particularly the suggestion made by the leader of this group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), when he urged that any special pay and allowances or other provisions that were to have been given to soldiers in the Pacific war should be given to these men, retroactive to the day they embarked in 1941, and that amounts due a deceased soldier should be given to his next of kin.
Mr. Speaker, as I understand it the purpose of this debate is to permit hon. members to discuss the government's proposals and activities in the light of what we believe to be the desires and the best interests of the people we represent. I shall endeavour to gear my remarks to that purpose. Perhaps before I launch into the main body of what I have to say I might offer the comment that it seems to me in this debate we have had more than we needed of rehashing the last election. Particularly has that been true of my hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party. Time and again they have simply rehashed what they thought were the issues in the election.

They won the election; yes, they won a majority of the seats in. this house, but one should take into consideration, and the government members especially should consider, the way the people of this country voted. Very well, I will give the figures. The people of western Canada sent to this house twenty-seven members of the C.C.F., nineteen members of the Liberal party, eleven members of the Progressive Conservative party, thirteen Social Creditors and two Independents.
I have made reference to these facts concerning the last election-and there are more I could give, particularly the soldier vote, which gave the C.C.F. first place overseas, but I had better watch my time-.not just for the amusement I seem to have caused but to suggest to the government that this is no time for complacency on their part. Not only have they serious problems with which to deal, but they have a country in which the majority of the people lack confidence in the present administration. They have a real task on their hands. They must deliver the goods.
Another reply that I feel we have had all too often from the government side of the house is that the war is just over; that V-E day was only in May and V-J day only in August; that the surrender of Japan was
The Address-Mr. Knowles

signed only two or three weeks ago, and we axe asked to be patient and give them time. Well, Mr. Speaker, that was not the attitude in September, 1939, when war broke out. There was a war to be won and something had to be done about it without delay. I suggest that peace has broken out and that the time to win the peace is now, before we lose it by allowing the problems of housing, insecurity and unemployment to pile up until their solution is made that much more difficult. So I urge that we have done with this complacency, with this stalling for time, and that the government get down to business and deal with the problems confronting the country right now while we are in session.
As I indicated earlier, I believe the purpose of this debate is to provide a chance for us to discuss some of the proposals the government has made. One of the fields in which we have had such proposals is that of social security. The other night the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Claxton) spoke on this matter, dealing particularly with old age pensions. He expressed great pleasure in the proposal that had been made of $30 a month for all those over seventy, and rejected any suggestion of a larger amount or a lower age limit on the ground that it would cost too much money, at the same time making the elaborate statement that Canada would soon lead the world in social security. In other words, every suggestion contained in the government's proposals is an admission that we have been right. They have now admitted we are right. Then why the delay? The government has power to make these increases and to make these changes now, and that is what the people of Canada are expecting.
The other night the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Claxton) said that we must be careful-I' am quoting from memory, but I think this is right-not to whet people's appetites and then find that we cannot satisfy their desires in connection with what they hope they are going to get. I want to tell him I am already having to answer letters from old people asking me if the new amount of $30 a month is to come into effect on January 1, 1946. They have the idea that this is something they will get while they are still alive. I have to write back to them to the effect that, no such announcement has been made by the government, but that we will do our best on the floor of the house to persuade the government to make such an announcement soon. If the minister meant what he said when he argued against whetting people's appetites for something they cannot be given, I suggest that he should pull all his weight toward bringing this $30 a month proposal into effect as soon as possible, because he has already whetted their appetites.

The Address-Mr. Knowles
Incidentally I want to say to the government that I am glad the administration of old age pensions has been transferred from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The result has been a sad story for old age pensioners. However, we now have a separate minister to argue with the Minister of Finance on behalf of old age pensioners. I believe he is interested in their welfare and I hope he will put up a real fight along the lines I am suggesting to-night.
Even when we get this $30 a month, which I hope we will get before 1048, I am afraid the Minister of National Health and Welfare will find that he must go still farther, if indeed he is going to achieve his ideal of a Canada leading the world in measures of social security. I suggest to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that his proposal of $30 a month at seventy years is hardly leading the world. The New Zealand benefit it at sixty and the new rate goes into effect this fall. I suggest, therefore, that Canada is hardly leading the world-although she will some day-in social security.
While I am speaking about what they are doing in New Zealand at the present time, may I point out that the parliament now in session in that country has before it a government measure to increase the benefits to be given to widows. In Canada we have no widow's benefits, except. mothers' allowances for widows with children. Even those allowances are only provincial in this country. The New Zealand government is increasing to one pound and ten shillings a week the benefit to widows. That is the equivalent, on the same basis I have outlined, of $44.46 a month in Canada.
A widow with two children will receive two pounds for herself and ten shillings for each child, making a total of three pounds a week or the equivalent in Canada on the same basis, of $88.92 a month.
In addition to these benefits, another im-crease is being made, and this time it is with respect to the special benefits given to wage earners who are sick or unemployed. This 
benefit is being increased to two pounds a week for the father, plus two pounds a week for the mother, plus ten shillings for each child. In other words, a family of four would receive five pounds a week when the wage-earner is unemployed either because of sickness or for some other cause. This, on the same basis I have already given, is the equivalent of $148.20 a month in Canada.
All this is being done in a country with only about 1,500,000 population, as compared with our 11,500,000. One has only to reflect upon that to realize the economic problem they must have in a country as small as that. It will be realized that their problem is much greater than ours, in our larger economic unit.
